questions.stem: Mr Clayton, 75, is seen in general practice with a left foot ulcer. After 10 minutes supine, brachial systolic pressures are 142 mmHg (right) and 138 mmHg (left); left dorsalis pedis is 80 mmHg and left posterior tibial 74 mmHg. The examiner asks you to explain how his left ankle-brachial index is calculated. Which calculation is correct?
options: 74 ÷ 138: lower left ankle pressure ÷ left arm pressure
80 ÷ 142: higher left ankle pressure ÷ higher arm pressure
80 ÷ 138: higher left ankle pressure ÷ left arm pressure
74 ÷ 142: lower left ankle pressure ÷ higher arm pressure
questions.why: The ABI for each leg is the higher of that leg's dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pressure divided by the higher brachial systolic pressure of the two arms. That gives 80/142 = 0.56 here, and 0.90 or below indicates peripheral arterial disease.
notes: Using the lower ankle pressure and the arm on the same side both lower the ratio and break the standard method.
The higher brachial pressure of the two arms is used, not the arm on the same side, because the higher one best reflects central aortic pressure.
The higher of the two ankle pressures for that leg is the numerator, not the lower.

questions.stem: Mr Clayton, 75, smoker with type 2 diabetes, has a 6-week painful punched-out ulcer over the left first MTP joint, a month of night forefoot pain eased by hanging the foot down, absent left pedal pulses, ABI 0.56 and left toe pressure 24 mmHg. No erythema, pus or fever; CRP is normal. Nothing has changed suddenly. What is the most appropriate disposition from general practice?
options: Routine vascular outpatient referral with GP review in 3 months
Wound swab, oral cefalexin and practice nurse review in one week
Urgent vascular surgery referral to be seen within days for imaging
Same-day ED transfer for an intravenous heparin infusion
questions.why: Rest pain or tissue loss with objectively confirmed arterial disease (toe pressure below 30 mmHg) is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia. He needs urgent vascular review within days for duplex imaging and to consider revascularisation, because the risk of amputation is high.
notes: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia carries a high amputation risk, so a routine referral with review months away is unsafe.
The ulcer shows no clinical signs of infection and CRP is normal, so a swab and antibiotics are not indicated and do nothing for the ischaemia.
An IV heparin infusion and same-day transfer are for acute limb ischaemia; his decline has been gradual, with normal sensation and movement.

questions.stem: Mr Clayton, 75, has moderate left peripheral arterial disease. For a month he has woken at night with forefoot pain that eases when he hangs his foot over the side of the bed or walks around, and is worse with his leg up on a pillow. Which mechanism best explains this pattern?
options: Dependency adds hydrostatic pressure, raising foot perfusion pressure beyond the stenoses
Dependency pools venous blood in the foot, lowering tissue metabolic oxygen demand
Dependency triggers a venoarteriolar reflex that dilates the foot arterioles
Dependency increases shear stress, releasing nitric oxide that dilates the stenosed artery
questions.why: Beyond fixed stenoses the distal perfusion pressure is only just enough. Lying flat or elevating the leg removes the hydrostatic column, so flow falls below resting needs and the foot hurts. Hanging the foot down restores that pressure, which is why patients with rest pain sleep with the leg dependent or in a chair.
notes: Venous pooling does not lower the foot's metabolic oxygen demand; the relief comes from higher arterial perfusion pressure.
The venoarteriolar reflex causes arteriolar vasoconstriction when the limb is dependent, not dilatation.
Atherosclerotic stenoses are fixed and respond little to endothelial nitric oxide; gravity, not flow-mediated dilatation, explains the relief.

questions.stem: Mr Clayton, 75, has a year of left calf claudication. On examination his left femoral pulse is palpable (weaker than the right, with a bruit) but the left popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent. Disease in which artery best explains the loss of the popliteal pulse with calf claudication?
options: Internal iliac artery in the pelvis
Profunda femoris artery in the thigh
Anterior tibial artery in the leg
Superficial femoral artery in the adductor canal
questions.why: A palpable femoral pulse with an absent popliteal pulse puts the lesion between the two, in the superficial femoral artery. Its distal segment at the adductor canal and hiatus is the commonest site of lower-limb atherosclerosis and classically causes calf claudication.
notes: Internal iliac disease causes buttock claudication and erectile dysfunction; this artery does not continue to the popliteal artery.
The profunda femoris supplies the thigh and is an important collateral route; blocking it alone would not abolish the popliteal pulse.
The anterior tibial artery arises below the popliteal artery, so disease there would leave the popliteal pulse intact.
